sectionTitle: Chemistry — Reversible reactions and dynamic equilibrium

specStatements.text: In some chemical reactions, the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. Such reactions are called reversible reactions and are represented:
A +B ⇌C + D
The direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions.
For example:
When a reversible reaction occurs in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.
The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.
If a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change.
The effects of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium can be predicted using Le Chatelier’s Principle.
Students should be able to make qualitative predictions about the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium when given appropriate information.

If the concentration of one of the reactants or products is changed, the system is no longer at equilibrium and the concentrations of all the substances will change until equilibrium is reached again.
If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.
If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.
Students should be able to interpret appropriate given data to predict the effect of a change in concentration of a reactant or product on given reactions at equilibrium.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is increased:
the relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction
the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an exothermic reaction.
If the temperature of a system at equilibrium is decreased:
the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction
the relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an exothermic reaction.
Students should be able to interpret appropriate given data to predict the effect of a change in temperature on given reactions at equilibrium.
For gaseous reactions at equilibrium:
an increase in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the smaller number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction
a decrease in pressure causes the equilibrium position to shift towards the side with the larger number of molecules as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.
Students should be able to interpret appropriate given data to predict the effect of pressure changes on given reactions at equilibrium.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to make qualitative predictions about the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium when given appropriate information.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every prediction asked for in this section is qualitative, and each stem supplies the information the prediction needs. Students are asked only which way the position of equilibrium moves and whether the amount of a named substance rises, falls or is unchanged. Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic in the forward direction, and the symbol equation from which molecules are counted, are always stated in the stem rather than assumed. No item asks for an equilibrium constant, a numerical yield or the size of a shift, and no item requires knowledge of a named industrial process, which the specification treats elsewhere.

The pressure rule is applied only to equilibria in which every substance is a gas, and each pressure question states the state symbols or says so explicitly. Molecules are counted only from the symbol equation given in the stem, as the specification requires. No item sets up an equilibrium that mixes gases with solids or liquids, and none asks students to decide which species count in such a mixture, which is beyond this specification.

concepts.definition: A reaction in which the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. Once some product has formed it is able to change back into the starting substances, so the change is not a one-way dead end.

The double arrow used to represent a reversible reaction, written A + B ⇌ C + D. It shows that the change can run in the forward direction and in the reverse direction; it does not say how much of each substance is present.
The specification's example of a reversible reaction: ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride. Heating the white solid gives the two gases, and cooling the gases forms the white solid again.
Apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, so that everything made by the forward reaction stays in the mixture and is available for the reverse reaction.

The state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate. Both reactions are still happening, so the amounts of the substances stay constant rather than becoming equal.

A description of the relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium. Moving towards the products is called shifting to the right; moving towards the reactants is shifting to the left.

The idea that if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, the system responds to counteract the change. It is used to predict the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium.
The system shifts in the direction that opposes what was done to it, reducing the effect of the change without cancelling it completely, so the new equilibrium is different from the original one.

If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products are formed until equilibrium is reached again; if the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants react until equilibrium is reached again.

Raising the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction and decreases it for an exothermic reaction. Lowering the temperature has the opposite effect in each case.

For gaseous reactions, an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules, and a decrease in pressure shifts it towards the side with the larger number.

concepts.term: Counting molecules from the symbol equation
concepts.definition: The numbers of gas molecules on each side of an equilibrium are read from the balancing numbers in the symbol equation, so 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 has three molecules on the left and two on the right.

misconceptions.question: A reversible reaction is written A + B ⇌ C + D. Does it run all the way forwards first, and only then run backwards?
misconceptions.correct: No. As soon as any C and D have formed they can react to give A and B back, so both changes happen in the same mixture at the same time.
misconceptions.misconception: A reversible reaction goes completely forwards until the reactants are used up, then turns round and goes completely backwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday reversible things are sequential - a swing goes out then comes back, a video plays then rewinds - so students import that one-after-the-other picture into chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants. That is possible from the moment any product exists, so the two directions overlap in time.

misconceptions.question: In A + B ⇌ C + D, does the ⇌ symbol tell you the mixture contains equal amounts of each substance?
misconceptions.correct: No. The symbol only shows that the reaction can go in both directions. It says nothing about how much of anything is present.
misconceptions.misconception: The double arrow means the reaction sits half-way, with the same amount of reactants as products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The arrow looks symmetrical and is often drawn with two arrows of equal length, which invites students to read symmetry in the picture as symmetry in the amounts.
misconceptions.correction: The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction, so they are usually not equal at all.

misconceptions.question: Once a reversible reaction has started in one direction, can its direction be changed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: The direction is fixed once the reaction starts, so a mixture can only ever go one way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most reactions students meet before this topic run to completion in one direction, so they treat direction as a permanent property of the reaction rather than something set by the conditions.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions, as when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and then has water added again.

misconceptions.question: At equilibrium, have the forward and reverse reactions stopped?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both reactions carry on, but at exactly the same rate, so the amounts of the substances do not change.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium is reached when the reactions stop and the mixture becomes chemically dead.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nothing appears to change once equilibrium is reached, and students take an unchanging observation to mean that nothing at all is happening.
misconceptions.correction: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate; a rate of zero is not what the specification describes.

misconceptions.question: At equilibrium, are the amounts of reactants and products equal?
misconceptions.correct: Not usually. The amounts stay constant, but the relative amounts depend on the conditions of the reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium means there is the same amount of reactant as product in the mixture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word equilibrium is used in everyday speech and in physics for balanced forces of equal size, so students expect equal quantities rather than equal rates.
misconceptions.correction: What is equal at equilibrium is the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction, not the amounts of the substances.

misconceptions.question: Can equilibrium be reached in an open beaker if one product is a gas?
misconceptions.correct: No. Equilibrium needs apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products.
misconceptions.misconception: Equilibrium is reached in any container, because the reverse reaction happens anyway.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students focus on the two reactions and overlook the apparatus, so the condition about preventing escape is treated as a detail rather than as part of the definition.
misconceptions.correction: If a product escapes it cannot take part in the reverse reaction, so the reverse rate can never rise to match the forward rate and equilibrium is never reached.

misconceptions.question: Does reaching equilibrium mean all of the reactants have been used up?
misconceptions.correct: No. Reactants and products are all present at equilibrium; their relative amounts depend on the conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: At equilibrium the reaction has finished, so only products are left in the container.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate the end of any observable change with the end of the reaction, which for one-way reactions usually does mean the reactants are gone.
misconceptions.correction: Both reactions are still occurring at equilibrium, which is only possible if reactants and products are both present in the mixture.

misconceptions.question: A condition is changed and the system counteracts the change. Does that put the condition back to its old value?
misconceptions.correct: No. The system reduces the effect of the change, but the new equilibrium is not the same as the old one.
misconceptions.misconception: Counteracting the change means the system undoes it completely and returns to its original state.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word counteract is read as cancel, and students who have met feedback in other subjects expect a system to restore its starting point exactly.
misconceptions.correction: The system responds to counteract the change, which shifts the position of equilibrium and gives new amounts of the substances rather than the original ones.

misconceptions.question: What can Le Chatelier's Principle be used to work out?
misconceptions.correct: The direction in which the position of equilibrium moves when a condition is changed.
misconceptions.misconception: It gives the exact amount of product formed once the new equilibrium has been reached.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students want a rule that produces a number, and the principle is introduced next to calculations on yield, so they expect it to be quantitative.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks only for qualitative predictions about the effect of changes on systems at equilibrium when appropriate information is given.

misconceptions.question: More reactant is added to a mixture at equilibrium. Which way does the position of equilibrium move?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the products. If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.
misconceptions.misconception: It moves towards the reactants, because that is the side that more substance was added to.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the equilibrium as tipping towards whichever side is made heavier, treating it as a balance of amounts rather than as a system that opposes the change.
misconceptions.correction: The system counteracts the increase by using up some of the added reactant, and using it up means forming more product.

misconceptions.question: A product is continuously removed from a mixture at equilibrium. What happens?
misconceptions.correct: More reactants react, so more product is formed until equilibrium is reached again.
misconceptions.misconception: The equilibrium moves towards the reactants, because there is now less product in the mixture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The same tipping-balance picture is used: less on the product side is read as the balance falling towards the reactant side.
misconceptions.correction: The system counteracts the loss by replacing some of the product, which means more reactants react and the position of equilibrium moves towards the products.

misconceptions.question: The concentration of one reactant is increased. Do the concentrations of the other substances change?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The concentrations of all the substances change until equilibrium is reached again.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the substance that was added ends up at a different concentration from before.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the substances as separate stores rather than as a linked system, so a change to one is not expected to reach the others.
misconceptions.correction: Once the system is no longer at equilibrium both reactions run at different rates, and that changes the concentrations of every substance in the mixture.

misconceptions.question: Does raising the temperature always increase the amount of product at equilibrium?
misconceptions.correct: No. It increases the relative amount of products for an endothermic reaction but decreases it for an exothermic reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating a reaction always gives more product, because heating makes reactions go better.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In rates work, raising the temperature always speeds a reaction up, and students carry that always-more result across to the amounts present at equilibrium.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature changes the position of equilibrium in a direction that depends on which way the reaction is exothermic, so the effect on the yield can go either way.

misconceptions.question: The forward reaction is exothermic. Which way does the equilibrium move when the temperature is raised?
misconceptions.correct: Towards the reactants, so the relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases.
misconceptions.misconception: Towards the products, because the forward reaction is the one that releases energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the system counteracts the change but then choose the direction that releases more energy into an already hotter system, reversing the logic.
misconceptions.correction: Adding energy is counteracted by taking energy in, so the endothermic direction is favoured; for an exothermic forward reaction that is the reverse direction.

misconceptions.question: Does cooling a system at equilibrium always reduce the amount of product?
misconceptions.correct: No. Cooling decreases the amount of products for an endothermic reaction and increases it for an exothermic one.
misconceptions.misconception: The student believes that cooling a reaction always increases the yield, because they think a lower temperature drives the reaction on towards the products.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cooling is associated with reactions slowing down and stopping, so students expect less of everything rather than a shift in position.
misconceptions.correction: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases on cooling for an exothermic reaction, which is why some industrial equilibria are run cool.

misconceptions.question: The pressure on a gaseous equilibrium is increased. Which side is favoured?
misconceptions.correct: The side with the smaller number of molecules, as shown by the symbol equation for that reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: The side with the larger number of molecules, because higher pressure makes more gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link high pressure with more gas being pushed into the vessel, and choose the side with more molecules without asking what would counteract the change.
misconceptions.correction: Fewer gas molecules exert less pressure, so shifting to the side with the smaller number of molecules is what counteracts an increase in pressure.

misconceptions.question: In 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, how do you decide which side has fewer molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Add the balancing numbers on each side: three molecules on the left and two on the right.
misconceptions.misconception: Compare the masses or the numbers of atoms rather than the numbers of molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Atom counting is drilled hard when balancing equations, so students reach for atoms, and mass is what they are used to conserving.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the number of molecules is shown by the symbol equation, which means the balancing numbers in front of each formula.

misconceptions.question: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). What happens to the position of equilibrium when the pressure is increased?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing. There are two gas molecules on each side, so neither side is favoured.
misconceptions.misconception: The equilibrium shifts, because a pressure change always moves the position of equilibrium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is remembered as pressure always has an effect, and students apply it without checking the numbers of molecules in the symbol equation.
misconceptions.correction: A pressure change shifts the position of equilibrium only where the two sides have different numbers of gas molecules.

misconceptions.question: A change is made to a system at equilibrium. Is a shift in position the same as a change in rate?
misconceptions.correct: No. A shift changes the relative amounts present at equilibrium, which is not the same as how fast equilibrium is reached.
misconceptions.misconception: The student does not distinguish the rate at which equilibrium is reached from the position of equilibrium, and so judges the amount of product from how a change affects the reaction's speed. Most often a change they regard as 'only a rate change' - such as cooling that merely slows both directions - is thought to leave the equilibrium amounts unchanged; the same confusion can make them treat the principle as a way of predicting how quickly equilibrium is reached, or lead them to assume that anything which speeds the reaction up must give more product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rates and equilibrium are taught side by side and both use the same conditions, so students merge going faster with going further.
misconceptions.correction: The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions, and a condition can change the rate without favouring either direction.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes what makes a reaction a reversible reaction?

options.text: The products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants
options.rationale: This is the definition given in the specification: in some chemical reactions the products can react to produce the original reactants.

options.text: The reaction goes fully forwards and then it goes fully backwards
options.rationale: Chosen by students who picture reversibility as one complete change followed by another, like a video rewinding.

options.text: The reaction finishes with equal amounts of reactants and products
options.rationale: Comes from reading reversible as meaning the two sides must end up balanced against each other.

options.text: The reaction can be made faster or slower by a change of conditions
options.rationale: Confuses a reaction whose direction can change with one whose rate can change; every reaction can be speeded up or slowed down.

mcqs.stem: A reversible reaction is represented as A + B ⇌ C + D. What does the ⇌ symbol tell you?

options.text: That the mixture holds equal amounts of A, B, C and D throughout it
options.rationale: Reads the symmetry of the drawn symbol as symmetry in the amounts; the symbol says nothing about how much of each substance is present.

options.text: That the reaction can go in the forward and the reverse direction
options.rationale: The double arrow is the way the specification represents a reversible reaction: A and B can form C and D, and C and D can form A and B.

options.text: That the mixture has already reached equilibrium at every moment
options.rationale: Confuses the symbol for a reversible reaction with the special state reached when the two rates become equal.

options.text: That the forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
options.rationale: Assumes an order of events; the symbol gives no information about which direction is faster at any time.

mcqs.stem: A sample of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated and turns white. What must be done to turn it blue again?

options.text: Nothing will work, as the direction is fixed once heating has started
options.rationale: Treats direction as a permanent property of a reaction rather than something set by the conditions.

options.text: Heat the white solid much more strongly for a longer period of time
options.rationale: Repeats the change that drove the reaction forwards, which cannot drive it back the other way.

options.text: Add water to the white solid, changing the conditions back again
options.rationale: The direction of reversible reactions can be changed by changing the conditions; adding water reverses the change that heating produced.

options.text: Grind the white solid to a powder to raise its surface area
options.rationale: Uses a rates idea; surface area affects how fast a reaction happens, not which direction a reversible reaction runs.

mcqs.stem: Ammonium chloride ⇌ ammonia + hydrogen chloride is given as an example of a reversible reaction. White ammonium chloride is heated in a tube and the two gases form. Which statement about this example is correct?

options.text: The ammonium chloride has been destroyed for good
options.rationale: Treats the decomposition as a one-way change, so the reverse direction is not expected to be available.

options.text: Half of the solid always stays behind unchanged
options.rationale: Reads the double arrow as meaning the reaction stops half-way, rather than as meaning both directions are possible.

options.text: The two gases must react first, before the solid heats
options.rationale: Imposes an order on the two directions instead of allowing them to happen in the same tube at the same time.

options.text: Cooling the gases re-forms ammonium chloride
options.rationale: The products react to produce the original reactant, which is what makes this the specification's example of a reversible reaction.

mcqs.stem: A reversible reaction takes place in a sealed flask. When is the mixture at equilibrium?

options.text: When both the forward and the reverse reactions have completely stopped
options.rationale: Takes an unchanging observation to mean nothing is happening; both reactions continue at equilibrium.

options.text: When the amounts of all the reactants and of all the products are the same
options.rationale: Reads equilibrium as equal quantities; what is equal is the rate of each reaction, not the amounts.

options.text: When all of the reactants have been converted into the products
options.rationale: Treats equilibrium as the end of a one-way reaction, leaving no reactants for the reverse change.

options.text: When the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of equilibrium in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products.

mcqs.stem: Why must a reversible reaction be carried out in apparatus that prevents reactants and products escaping if equilibrium is to be reached?

options.text: Escaped products cannot take part in reverse reactions
options.rationale: The reverse rate can only rise to match the forward rate if the products stay in the mixture, so escape prevents equilibrium.

options.text: The reverse reaction happens anyway, whatever escapes
options.rationale: From m08: the student thinks the reverse reaction is reached in any container regardless of whether products escape, so denies that preventing escape matters - a plausible but wrong answer to why sealed apparatus is needed.

options.text: Equilibrium means nothing at all is allowed to move about
options.rationale: Reads the closed apparatus as a way of stopping the reactions rather than of keeping the substances together.

options.text: The reactants and products must be present in equal amounts
options.rationale: Brings in an equal-amounts idea, which is not why the apparatus has to be closed.

mcqs.stem: The same reversible reaction is allowed to reach equilibrium at two different temperatures. What can be said about the amounts of the substances present?

options.text: The amounts must be equal at equilibrium whatever conditions are used
options.rationale: Applies the equal-amounts misreading of equilibrium, which would leave no role for the conditions.

options.text: The amounts depend only on how quickly equilibrium was reached
options.rationale: Confuses how quickly a system arrives at equilibrium with where the equilibrium position lies.

options.text: The relative amounts of the reactants and products depend on the conditions
options.rationale: The specification states that the relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.

options.text: The amounts are fixed by the masses that were mixed at the start
options.rationale: Treats the outcome as set at the beginning, so changing the conditions is expected to make no difference.

mcqs.stem: A system at equilibrium has one of its conditions changed. According to the specification, how does the system respond?

options.text: It responds until the change made to it has been cancelled out completely
options.rationale: Reads counteract as cancel; the system reduces the effect of the change but does not undo it.

options.text: It stays exactly as it was, because it is already at equilibrium
options.rationale: Treats equilibrium as a frozen state that cannot respond to anything.

options.text: It stops reacting until the original conditions are restored
options.rationale: Again assumes the reactions can switch off; both continue while the system responds.

options.text: It responds in the direction that counteracts the change that was made
options.rationale: If a system at equilibrium has a condition changed, the system responds to counteract the change.

mcqs.stem: What can Le Chatelier's Principle be used for?

options.text: Predicting the effect of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium
options.rationale: The effects of changing conditions on a system at equilibrium can be predicted using Le Chatelier's Principle.

options.text: Calculating the exact amount of each product present at the new equilibrium
options.rationale: Expects a quantitative result; the specification asks only for qualitative predictions.

options.text: Predicting how long a given mixture will take to reach equilibrium again
options.rationale: Confuses the position of equilibrium with the rate at which it is reached.

options.text: Showing that heating a reaction always increases its yield
options.rationale: From m15: the student over-generalises that heating always gives more product, so thinks Le Chatelier's Principle is used to demonstrate that heating always boosts yield.

mcqs.stem: In a sealed flask N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The forward reaction is exothermic. More nitrogen is pumped into the flask at constant temperature. What is the qualitative prediction?

options.text: Less ammonia is present at the new equilibrium
options.rationale: Tips the balance towards the side that was added to, instead of towards the side that uses the addition up.

options.text: More ammonia forms at the new equilibrium
options.rationale: Increasing the concentration of a reactant means more products are formed until equilibrium is reached again.

options.text: The amount of ammonia present cannot change
options.rationale: Assumes the system restores its original state exactly rather than settling at a new equilibrium.

options.text: Ammonia forms faster but its amount is fixed
options.rationale: Separates rate from position correctly in words but then denies the shift that the added reactant causes.

mcqs.stem: The concentration of one substance in a mixture at equilibrium is changed. What happens to the concentrations of the other substances?

options.text: Only the substance whose concentration was altered is different
options.rationale: Treats the substances as separate stores rather than as one linked system.

options.text: They stay the same, as the system is always at equilibrium
options.rationale: Assumes equilibrium is permanent, so no change can disturb it.

options.text: They change only when the temperature is altered as well
options.rationale: Restricts shifts to temperature changes, ignoring the effect of concentration.

options.text: They all change until equilibrium is reached again in the mixture
options.rationale: The system is no longer at equilibrium, and the concentrations of all the substances change until equilibrium is reached again.

mcqs.stem: For the equilibrium CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O, more ethanol (C2H5OH) is added. What happens?

options.text: More products form until equilibrium is reached again in the flask
options.rationale: If the concentration of a reactant is increased, more products will be formed until equilibrium is reached again.

options.text: More reactants form, because ethanol was added to the reactant side
options.rationale: Chooses the side that was added to, treating the equilibrium as a balance of amounts.

options.text: Nothing changes at all, since the total mass has not altered
options.rationale: Expects the system to cancel the change completely and return to its original state.

options.text: The reaction speeds up but no extra ester is being formed
options.rationale: Recognises a rate effect but denies the change in the relative amounts at equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: In the equilibrium 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, sulfur trioxide (SO3) is continuously removed from the mixture. What happens?

options.text: More reactants form, because there is now less product present
options.rationale: Tips the balance towards the reactants because that side now looks heavier.

options.text: More reactants react until equilibrium is reached again
options.rationale: If the concentration of a product is decreased, more reactants will react until equilibrium is reached again.

options.text: Nothing happens, because the system stays at equilibrium
options.rationale: Assumes a system at equilibrium cannot respond to a change made to it.

options.text: The mixture ends up holding equal amounts of each one
options.rationale: Falls back on the idea that equilibrium means equal amounts of each substance.

mcqs.stem: A sealed flask holds an equilibrium mixture of hydrogen, iodine and hydrogen iodide: H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI. Extra hydrogen is injected and the flask is left until equilibrium is reached again. What is found?

options.text: Less HI, and more iodine than there was before
options.rationale: Shifts towards the side that hydrogen was added to, which is the opposite of counteracting the change.

options.text: The same HI and the same iodine as before
options.rationale: Assumes only the added substance has a new concentration and the rest are untouched.

options.text: More HI, and less iodine than there was
options.rationale: Increasing a reactant concentration forms more product, and forming more HI uses up some of the iodine.

options.text: Only the hydrogen is now at a higher level than before
options.rationale: From m14: the student believes only the substance that was added (hydrogen) changes concentration, so predicts hydrogen is higher while HI and iodine are unchanged.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is increased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It increases, because the reaction is endothermic in the forward direction
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an endothermic reaction when the temperature is increased.

options.text: It decreases, because raising the temperature will release more energy
options.rationale: Chooses the direction that would give out energy into an already hotter system, reversing the reasoning.

options.text: It decreases, because the reactants are used up much more quickly
options.rationale: Confuses using the reactants up faster with ending up with less product once equilibrium is reached again.

options.text: It stays the same, because heating changes only the reaction rates
options.rationale: Applies a rates-only rule and misses the change in position of equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is increased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It increases, because the forward reaction is the exothermic one
options.rationale: Favours the direction that releases energy, which is not what counteracts a rise in temperature.

options.text: It decreases, because the forward reaction gives out energy
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an exothermic reaction when the temperature is increased.

options.text: It increases, since heating always improves any yield
options.rationale: Carries an always-more rule across from rates work to the amounts at equilibrium.

options.text: It stays the same, since heating changes only the rates
options.rationale: Treats temperature as affecting speed alone, which is true for a one-way reaction but not here.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is endothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is decreased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It increases, as cooling a mixture always drives the reaction onwards
options.rationale: Applies a blanket rule about cooling instead of using the direction of the energy transfer.

options.text: It increases, as the system must give out energy when it cools down
options.rationale: Picks the exothermic direction correctly for cooling but forgets that here it is the reverse reaction.

options.text: It decreases, as the endothermic direction is no longer favoured
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium decreases for an endothermic reaction when the temperature is decreased.

options.text: It stays the same, as cooling only slows both reactions down
options.rationale: Reduces a temperature change to a rate effect and misses the shift in position.

mcqs.stem: The forward reaction of a reversible reaction is exothermic. The temperature of the system at equilibrium is decreased. What happens to the relative amount of products?

options.text: It decreases, as a cooler mixture must form less product
options.rationale: Uses a blanket cooling-lowers-yield rule rather than the direction of the energy transfer.

options.text: It decreases, as the endothermic direction is favoured
options.rationale: Chooses the endothermic direction, which is what counteracts heating rather than cooling.

options.text: It stays the same, as cooling alters only the two rates
options.rationale: Treats cooling as a rate effect only, missing the change in the relative amounts.

options.text: It increases, as the forward reaction is exothermic
options.rationale: The relative amount of products at equilibrium increases for an exothermic reaction when the temperature is decreased.

mcqs.stem: For 2NO2 ⇌ N2O4 the forward reaction is exothermic. A sealed tube of the mixture is placed in iced water and the brown colour of NO2 fades. What does this show?

options.text: Cooling has stopped both of the reactions in the sealed tube
options.rationale: Reads the steady pale colour as evidence that the reactions have switched off.

options.text: Cooling has increased the relative amount of the product N2O4
options.rationale: Lowering the temperature increases the relative amount of products for an exothermic reaction, so the brown NO2 is used up.

options.text: Cooling has moved the equilibrium towards the reactant NO2
options.rationale: Applies cooling-lowers-yield, which would deepen rather than fade the brown colour.

options.text: Cooling has slowed the forward reaction down only
options.rationale: Explains the observation as a rate change, which would not alter the amounts at equilibrium.

mcqs.stem: For the gaseous equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), the pressure is increased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?

options.text: Towards nitrogen and hydrogen, the side with more molecules
options.rationale: Links higher pressure with more gas molecules instead of asking what would counteract the increase.

options.text: Neither way, as pressure cannot alter this mixture
options.rationale: Assumes pressure has no effect, though the two sides have different numbers of molecules.

options.text: Towards the ammonia, the side with the fewer molecules
options.rationale: An increase in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the smaller number of molecules: four on the left, two on the right.

options.text: Towards the nitrogen, which has heavier molecules
options.rationale: Compares relative masses instead of counting the numbers of molecules shown by the symbol equation.

mcqs.stem: For the gaseous equilibrium 2SO3(g) ⇌ 2SO2(g) + O2(g), the pressure is decreased. Which way does the equilibrium position shift?

options.text: To the left, towards the side with just two gas molecules
options.rationale: Reverses the rule and moves towards the smaller number of molecules when the pressure falls.

options.text: Neither way, since the numbers of atoms are equal here
options.rationale: Counts atoms, which are always equal in a balanced equation, instead of molecules.

options.text: Neither way, as pressure changes only alter rates
options.rationale: Treats a pressure change as a rate effect alone, so no shift in the relative amounts is expected.

options.text: To the right, the side with three molecules of gas
options.rationale: A decrease in pressure shifts the position towards the side with the larger number of molecules: two on the left, three on the right.

mcqs.stem: A student is given the equilibrium H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), all gases, and increases the pressure on the sealed vessel. What should the student predict?

options.text: No shift, as each side has two molecules
options.rationale: The sides have equal numbers of gas molecules, so neither side is favoured by a change in pressure.

options.text: A shift to the right, towards the hydrogen iodide
options.rationale: Applies the pressure rule without first counting the molecules in the symbol equation.

options.text: A shift to the left, towards hydrogen and iodine
options.rationale: Assumes pressure must always move the position of equilibrium one way or the other.

options.text: A shift to the side with the heavier molecules
options.rationale: Uses relative masses in place of the numbers of molecules given by the equation.
